claim: Neural execution of graph algorithms: an MPNN with max aggregator, trained on 20-node graphs, predicts reachability (BFS) at 100 nodes with 99.80% last-step accuracy.
notes: Train 20 nodes, test 20/50/100. Baselines LSTM, GAT, GAT-full (Transformer-like), MPNN-mean/sum. Parameter/FLOP matching not stated -> unmatched.

claim: Same table: fully-connected attention (GAT-full, labelled Vaswani et al. 2017) reaches only 91.51% last-step reachability accuracy at 100 nodes vs MPNN-max 99.80%, trained at 20 nodes.
notes: Evidence against dense attention as substitute for sparse task graph on reachability; unmatched (params/FLOPs not reported).

claim: MPNN-mean collapses out of distribution on reachability: 21.40% last-step accuracy at 100 nodes after 100% at 20 nodes, i.e. aggregator choice decides size extrapolation.
notes: Failure evidence: in-distribution 100% says nothing about size generalisation. Unmatched.

claim: Neural execution uses a learned termination network that decides when to stop iterating (a learned halt), capped at |V| steps.
locator: Sec. 3 (termination network T_A) and Sec. 4 training
quote: If the termination network TA does not terminate the neural network computation within |V | steps, it is assumed terminated at that point.
notes: Prior art for C12 (learned halting) inside a GNN executor.

claim: Neural execution authors hypothesise max-aggregation MPNNs are best suited to graph algorithms because they rely on discrete neighbourhood decisions.
quote: we hypothesise that maximisation-based message passing neural networks are bestsuited for such objectives, and validate this claim empirically.

claim: CLRS-30 protocol: train and validate on 16-node inputs (1,000 training trajectories), test out-of-distribution on 64-node inputs (4x larger).
quote: we sample inputs of 16 nodes for both, and generate 1,000 trajectories for training and 32 for validation. For testing, we measure out-of-distribution generalisation, and sample 32 trajectories for inputs of 64 nodes.
notes: The canonical NAR size ladder is only 4x; prereg asks >=4x.

claim: CLRS-30 baseline: MPNN overall OOD (64-node) average micro-F1 44.99%, PGN 50.84%.
notes: Columns: Deep Sets, GAT, Memnet, MPNN, PGN. FLOPs not matched.

claim: CLRS-30 authors: MPNNs are unable to transfer their in-distribution gains to graphs four times larger; PGN becomes best on average OOD.
quote: MPNNs are unable to transfer their impressive gains to graphs that are four times larger: in fact, the PGN takes over as the most performant model when averaged across task types
notes: Failure evidence for size generalisation of dense message passing.

claim: CLRS-30 sorting class OOD: MPNN averages only 11.83% micro-F1 while Memory Networks get 71.53%.
notes: Columns Deep Sets/GAT/Memnet/MPNN/PGN. Unmatched FLOPs.

claim: CLRS-30 string algorithms are essentially unsolved OOD by all baselines (MPNN 3.21% micro-F1).
notes: Failure evidence.

claim: Triplet-GMPNN (gated MPNN with triplet edge messages) reaches 74.14% overall OOD micro-F1 on CLRS-30 vs 50.84% for the best prior baseline (PGN).
notes: Columns Memnet/MPNN/PGN/Triplet-GMPNN; train 16 nodes, test 64. Not param- or FLOP-matched (triplet messages are O(n^3)).

claim: Triplet-GMPNN exceeds 90% OOD accuracy on only 11 of 30 CLRS algorithms.
quote: we now exceed 60% accuracy in 24 algorithms (15 algorithms previously), 80% for 17 algorithms (9 previously) and 90% for 11 algorithms (6 previously).
notes: Even best processor misses the prereg 0.95 bar on most algorithms at 4x size.

claim: Triplet reasoning computes a message for every node triplet then max-reduces to edge latents (Floyd-Warshall-style edge updates).
quote: we introduce triplet reasoning: first, computing representations over triplets of nodes, then reducing over one node to obtain edge latents
notes: O(n^3) per step: relevant to GPU cost (V5).

claim: Generalist learner adds a per-node update gate because algorithms update few nodes per step; gate helps single-task but not multi-task.
quote: We found that the gate stabilizes learning on many of the tasks, and increases the mean performance over all tasks on single-task training significantly. Surprisingly, however, we did not find gating to be advantageous in the multi-task case.
notes: Relevant to C4 stability fixes.

claim: Triplet-GMPNN still fails some CLRS tasks OOD: Quickselect 0.47% micro-F1.
notes: Failure evidence; last column Triplet-GMPNN.

claim: Pointer Graph Networks let each node dynamically point to another node and message-pass over those inferred pointer edges, i.e. edges are created at inference.
quote: PGNs allow each node to dynamically point to another node, followed by message passing over these pointers. The sparsity of this adaptable graph structure makes learning tractable
notes: Closest prior art for C6/C8/C13 (state-conditioned edge creation per step).

claim: PGN pointers are learned with direct supervision from classical data-structure traces, not discovered unsupervised.
quote: Critically, the pointing mechanism is directly supervised to model long-term sequences of operations on classical data structures
notes: Key gap: unsupervised top-k edge creation (candidate C6) is not what PGN shows.

claim: PGNs generalise to 5x larger inputs on dynamic graph connectivity, beating unrestricted GNNs and Deep Sets.
quote: PGNs generalise out-of-distribution to 5× larger test inputs on dynamic graph connectivity tasks, outperforming unrestricted GNNs and Deep Sets.
notes: Unmatched; baselines are GNNs and Deep Sets, no Transformer/looped baseline.

claim: Neural Execution Engines: plain seq2seq Transformers learn sorting but degrade as lists grow beyond training length.
quote: transformer-based sequence-to-sequence models can learn subroutines like sorting a list of numbers, but their performance rapidly degrades as the length of lists grows beyond those found in the training set.
notes: Failure evidence for dense attention on length extrapolation.

claim: NEE (Transformer with learned conditional mask/pointer) trained on length <=8 sorts length-100 sequences.
quote: strongly generalize on merge sort over long sequences (up to length 100) while trained on sequences of length smaller or equal to 8.
notes: Requires subroutine-level supervision and binary number encoding; no param matching reported.

claim: NEE is described as a graph attention network that modifies its own graph (mask) via predicted pointers, applied iteratively.
quote: A NEE is essentially a graph attention network [27] that can modify its own graph, resulting in a new decoding mechanism.
notes: Prior art for C13 inside a Transformer.

claim: Deep Thinking (Schwarzschild 2021): recurrent nets trained on easy instances solve harder ones by running more iterations at test time without new parameters; feed-forward nets cannot.
quote: we find that the performance of recurrent models improves as they recur for more iterations, even without adding parameters or re-training in the new, more challenging problem domain.
notes: Core 'time replaces depth' prior result; convolutional grid, not a graph.

claim: Deep Thinking prefix-sum protocol: train on 32-bit strings, test on 40- and 44-bit strings; effective depths 40-68 layers.
quote: We train models on easy data consisting of 32-bit input strings and test on harder 40-bit and 44-bit strings.
notes: Recurrent vs feed-forward compared at equal effective depth (recurrent has fewer params) -> depth-matched, not param-matched.

claim: DT-Recall with progressive loss, trained on 32-bit prefix sums with at most 30 recurrent iterations, solves 512-bit strings at 97.12% peak accuracy (237 test iterations); plain DT gets 11.26%, FF 0.00%.
notes: 16x length extrapolation. Baselines DT (same recurrence, no recall) and FF; FF is depth-matched to training iterations, not param-matched. Peak accuracy chosen post hoc over iterations (selection on test curve).

claim: DT-Recall trained on 9x9 mazes solves 59x59 mazes at 97.30% peak accuracy after 984 test iterations; plain DT and feed-forward get 0.00% at 59x59.
locator: Appendix A.5, Table 4 (Tested on 59 x 59 Mazes)
notes: ~6.5x side length. Needs ~1000 iterations: inference compute grows with size. Unmatched FLOPs vs FF.

claim: Overthinking: recurrent thinking nets degrade when iterated far beyond their training regime; fix is 'recall' (re-inject input every step) plus a progressive loss over random iteration counts.
quote: We observe that this approach fails to scale to highly complex problems because behavior degenerates when many iterations are applied – an issue we refer to as "overthinking." We propose a recall architecture that keeps an explicit copy of the problem instance in memory
notes: Stability failure mode + fix directly relevant to V4 (T_test=4xT_train). Candidate must include input re-injection or equivalent.

claim: Chess puzzles show a ceiling: DT-Recall peaks at 82.69% vs feed-forward 61.17% on harder (600K-700K) puzzles; extra iterations do not close the gap to 100%.
notes: Evidence that iteration helps but saturates on a task not decomposable into a local iterative rule. FF baseline unmatched in params.

claim: Ablation: a loss that directly penalises run time (loss weights increasing with iteration) gave maze models that solved 0 of the 59x59 test mazes despite >99% training accuracy and 93.8% at 33x33.
quote: On maze data, these models were not able to solve any 59x59 mazes in our test set, and we note that the training accuracy is >99% and the accuracy on 33x33 mazes is 93.8%
notes: Failure evidence: training variants that change the iteration objective can destroy extrapolation. Exact variant described in the appendix paragraph preceding the quote.

claim: Uncanny Similarity of Recurrence and Depth: weight-tied recurrent nets emulate deep feed-forward nets' hierarchical behaviour, often with far fewer parameters.
quote: we show that recurrent networks have the ability to closely emulate the behavior of non-recurrent deep models, often doing so with far fewer parameters.
notes: Supports 'computational capacity per parameter' half of hypothesis; not about knowledge storage.

claim: Recurrent ResNet-18 analogues perform nearly as well as ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/SVHN/EMNIST with about one third of the parameters.
quote: Table 1 shows that these recurrent models perform nearly as well as ResNet-18, despite containing only a third of the parameters.
notes: Depth-matched (effective depth), not FLOP-different: FLOPs roughly equal, params 1/3.

claim: Maze extrapolation critique (2024): pretrained DT-Net and PI-Net extrapolate in maze size but fail along other difficulty axes (cycles via percolation, deadend start).
quote: By varying test data along multiple axes — not just maze size — we show that models introduced in prior work fail in a variety of ways, some expected and others less so. It remains uncertain whether any of these models has truly learned an algorithm.
notes: Adversarial evidence: size-extrapolation success can be a narrow algorithm (deadend-filling) that breaks on mazes with loops.

claim: DT-Net's maze outputs agree with the classical deadend-filling algorithm on 98.8% of 143k test mazes, including its failures.
quote: the output of the RNN agrees with deadend-filling on 98.8% of 143k tests mazes across a variety of sizes and percolation values.
notes: Deadend-filling fails on mazes with cycles -> learned algorithm is not shortest-path in general.

claim: DT-Net accuracy rapidly diminishes as maze percolation (cycles) rises above 0, and extra iterations do not change outputs.
quote: The accuracy of DT-Net rapidly diminishes when percolation increases above 0. DT-Net was iterated 30 times, and the resulting outputs do not change with additional iterations.
notes: Failure evidence for V4: more iterations do not rescue distribution shift other than size.

claim: Training on more diverse mazes fixes some failures but paradoxically does not improve logical extrapolation; non-fixed-point models can enter limit cycles.
quote: training these models on more diverse data addresses some failure modes but, paradoxically, does not improve logical extrapolation. We also analyze convergence behavior, and show that models explicitly trained to converge to a fixed point are likely to do so
notes: Convergence signal (C11) is not a correctness signal: limit cycles occur even when correct.

claim: Prior maze extrapolation work fixed percolation=0 and deadend start=True for both train and test — a narrow distribution that admits a deadend-filling shortcut.
quote: Prior work (Bansal et al. 2022; Anil et al. 2022) has set percolation = 0 and deadend start = True for both training and testing.
notes: Benchmark pitfall: our maze family must vary percolation and start position, not only size.

claim: PI-Net (implicit/DEQ maze solver) failed on all 49x49 mazes with the original Broyden threshold 40; needed threshold 1,000, raising memory cost.
quote: it appears the threshold parameter was originally set at 40. However, with this setting PI-Net performed very poorly; it failed on all mazes of size 49 × 49.
notes: Implicit-model extrapolation is solver-hyperparameter sensitive; memory scales with threshold.

claim: NeuralSolver: recurrent solver for same-size and different-size tasks, claims better extrapolation than prior recurrent solvers with fewer parameters.
quote: NeuralSolver consistently outperforms the prior state-ofthe-art recurrent solvers in extrapolating to larger problems, considering smaller training problems and requiring less parameters than other approaches.
notes: Baselines are recurrent solvers (DT family), not Transformers.

claim: CLRS-Text: procedural generator converting CLRS-30 graph traces to text; a single Gemma 2B is trained on chosen sizes for all thirty algorithms and evaluated in interpolation and extrapolation regimes.
quote: we follow a rigorous out-of-distribution setup, wherein we pre-train a Gemma 2B model (Gemma Team et al., 2024) using the standard next-token prediction objective on specific problem sizes across all thirty algorithms
notes: Language-track benchmark for the later 'language' phase.

claim: CLRS-Text authors flag contamination: CLRS algorithms are standard textbook material with implementations omnipresent on GitHub, likely in frontier-model training data.
quote: their implementations are omnipresent on GitHub, and it is very likely that most frontier models have been trained on such source codes.
notes: Pitfall: leakage for pretrained-LM baselines; irrelevant for from-scratch matched arms.

claim: SALSA-CLRS: sparse extension of CLRS (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Eccentricity, MIS, MST) evaluated on graphs up to 100x the training size; CLRS's fully connected execution model causes OOM on large graphs.
unit: x training graph size at test
quote: SALSA-CLRS enables the evaluation of scalable architectures on graphs up to 100 times the size of the training graphs.
notes: Recommended generator for reachability/shortest-path ladders beyond 4x.

claim: SALSA-CLRS: RecGNN trained on ER graphs n<=16 keeps BFS node accuracy 99.2% at n=1600 on ER graphs, but drops to 55.6% on Delaunay graphs at n=1600.
locator: Table 1 (BFS rows, ER and Delaunay columns)
notes: Columns ER 16/80/160/800/1600, WS same, Delaunay same. Node accuracy, not graph-level exact match. Baselines GIN(E), PGN; no Transformer; unmatched.

claim: SALSA-CLRS: DFS is not learned by any sparse model even in distribution (PGN 74.2% node acc at n=16, 25.8% at n=1600 on ER).
notes: Failure evidence: sequential/stack algorithms resist message passing.

claim: SALSA-CLRS: graph-level Eccentricity accuracy for PGN falls from 100.0% to 0.0% on Delaunay graphs at n=800-1600; node-level metrics hide graph-level failure.
notes: Supports prereg's use of exact-match (graph-level) accuracy.

claim: TransNAR: Transformer tokens cross-attend to node embeddings of a pre-trained GNN reasoner; reports >20% absolute OOD gains in several CLRS-Text algorithm classes over Transformer-only.
quote: TransNAR enables emerging capabilities in the particular out-of-distribution regime depicted here, with over 20% absolute improvement in several of the algorithm classes.
notes: Baseline: Transformer-only LM of same backbone; the NAR adds parameters and a graph input, so not param-matched.

claim: No-hint NAR (Rodionov & Prokhorenkova 2023): removing trajectory supervision and adding a self-supervised regulariser is competitive with hint-supervised models; sorting F1 98.7% vs prior best 95.2%.
quote: we get the F1 score 98.7% for the sorting, which significantly improves over the previously known winner with 95.2%.
notes: Baseline: hint-supervised Triplet-GMPNN family; same processor, not FLOP-matched. Relevant: candidate need not rely on hints.

claim: Models trained without hints tend toward parallel processing, so imitating the sequential trajectory can be suboptimal.
quote: the model trained without hint supervision has a greater tendency to do parallel processing, thus following the original sequential trajectory can be suboptimal.

claim: Hint-ReLIC (causal regularisation via data augmentation on hints) reports up to 3x improvement on CLRS OOD test data.
quote: We evaluate our method on the CLRS algorithmic reasoning benchmark, where we show up to 3× improvements on the OOD test data.
notes: Baseline Triplet-GMPNN; same processor, not FLOP-matched.

claim: Discrete NAR forces execution through finite predefined discrete states; with state-transition supervision it achieves perfect test scores and provable correctness for any test size.
quote: Trained with supervision on the algorithm’s state transitions, such models are able to perfectly align with the original algorithm. To show this, we evaluate our approach on multiple algorithmic problems and achieve perfect test scores
notes: Strong size generalisation comes from heavy supervision + discretisation, not from free latent dynamics; a confound for the candidate.

claim: Recurrent NAR (LSTM aggregator instead of symmetric max) reaches 87% mean micro-F1 on Quickselect, where Triplet-GMPNN had 0.47%.
quote: RNAR achieves a mean micro-F1 score of 87%.
notes: Same architecture except aggregator: an ablation-style, roughly param-comparable comparison (exact counts not stated).

claim: CLRS: ten of thirty tasks are sequential (list inputs with natural order), where permutation-invariant aggregation is a mismatch.
quote: Indeed, such algorithms are frequent in CLRS—ten out of thirty of its tasks [19–23] are sequential.
notes: Ordered/sequence tasks may favour Transformer/RNN arms over a symmetric graph arm.

claim: Positional Transformers (attention weights depend only on positional encodings) keep the expressivity of parallel computational models at a logarithmic depth cost in input length.
quote: We prove that Transformers with positional attention (positional Transformers) maintain the same expressivity of parallel computational models, incurring a logarithmic depth cost relative to the input length.
notes: Fixed (input-independent) routing suffices for many parallel algorithms: weakens the necessity of state-conditioned topology (C8).

claim: Nerem et al. 2025: a min-aggregation GNN minimising a sparsity-regularised loss on a small set of shortest-path instances provably implements Bellman-Ford and extrapolates to graphs of any size.
quote: these GNNs are guaranteed to extrapolate to arbitrary shortest-path problems, including instances of any size.
notes: Guarantee requires L0/sparsity regulariser and MinAgg architecture aligned to BF.

claim: Which Algorithms Can GNNs Learn? (2026): sufficient conditions for MPNNs to learn from small instances and provably approximate on any size (SSSP, MST, DP incl. 0-1 knapsack), plus impossibility results for many tasks.
quote: we establish impossibility results for a wide range of algorithmic tasks, showing that standard MPNNs cannot learn them and derive more expressive MPNN-like architectures that overcome these limitations.
notes: Shared M/U message passing has provable learnability limits: an explicit constraint on the candidate's message function.

claim: Recursive algorithmic reasoning: GNNs cannot execute recursive algorithms without arbitrarily large memory; augmenting a GNN with a stack improves size generalisation on DFS.
quote: neural networks are currently unable to execute recursive algorithms because they do not have arbitrarily large memory to store and recall state. To address this, we (1) propose a way to augment graph neural networks (GNNs) with a stack
notes: Supports C9 (external/associative memory) as necessary for some algorithm classes.

claim: Algorithmic alignment: a network learns a reasoning task with lower sample complexity when its computation structure aligns with the algorithm; GNNs align with dynamic programming.
quote: We formally define this algorithmic alignment and derive a sample complexity bound that decreases with better alignment.
notes: Theory basis for why task-graph GNNs beat Transformers on DP tasks.

claim: How NNs extrapolate: ReLU MLPs converge to linear functions away from the data; GNN algorithmic extrapolation relies on encoding task-specific non-linearities (e.g. min/max aggregation).
quote: the success of GNNs in extrapolating algorithmic tasks to new data (e.g., larger graphs or edge weights) relies on encoding task-specific non-linearities in the architecture or features.
notes: Shared M/U with generic MLPs is not expected to extrapolate without aligned aggregators.

claim: Size generalisation in GNNs: when local structures differ between small and large graphs, there exist 'bad' global minima that fit small graphs but fail on large ones.
quote: GNNs are not guaranteed to generalize across sizes: there are ”bad” global minima that do well on small graphs but fail on large graphs.
notes: Failure evidence; the size ladder must keep local degree statistics comparable or report shift.

claim: GNNs are Dynamic Programmers: category-theory/abstract-algebra argument for an intricate connection between GNNs and DP beyond Bellman-Ford.
quote: we show, using methods from category theory and abstract algebra, that there exists an intricate connection between GNNs and DP, going well beyond the initial observations over individual algorithms such as Bellman-Ford.

claim: Parallel algorithms align with neural execution: NAR processors are parallel, so teaching sequential algorithms wastes computation; parallel variants need fewer layers and train faster.
quote: Parallel algorithms however may exploit their full computational power, therefore requiring fewer layers to be executed. This drastically reduces training times
notes: Iteration budget T should be set by parallel depth of the task, not sequential step count.

claim: ForgetNet: historical embeddings (persistent hidden states across steps) contradict the Markov nature of algorithm execution; ForgetNet drops them, G-ForgetNet gates them back in for early training.
quote: such historical dependence intrinsically contradicts the Markov nature of algorithmic reasoning tasks. Based on this motivation, we present our ForgetNet, which does not use historical embeddings
notes: Adversarial evidence against C1 (persistent latent node state) when step-wise hints define the state.

claim: Sanford et al. 2024: logarithmic depth is necessary and sufficient for Transformers to solve graph connectivity; single-layer Transformers with small embeddings solve contextual retrieval.
locator: Abstract; Sec. 3 (Hardness taxonomy of transformer graph reasoning tasks)
quote: We prove that logarithmic depth is necessary and sufficient for tasks like graph connectivity, while single-layer transformers with small embedding dimensions can solve contextual retrieval tasks.
notes: Implication: a looped Transformer needs only O(log n) iterations for reachability, whereas message passing over a sparse task graph needs O(diameter). The candidate's iteration budget is at a structural disadvantage on connectivity unless it creates long-range edges.

claim: Sanford et al. generalise the result that graph connectivity is computed more depth-efficiently by Transformers than by GNNs.
quote: We generalize the insights of [69]—which established that graph connectivity can be computed in a more depth-efficient manner with transformers than GNNs—to broader families of graph reasoning tasks.
notes: Directly supports the 'Transformer is already a better graph' objection on reachability.

claim: Transformers Struggle to Learn to Search: with the right (balanced) training distribution Transformers learn graph search, but difficulty grows with input graph size and is not fixed by more parameters or by chain-of-thought.
quote: as the input graph size increases, the transformer has greater difficulty in learning the task. This difficulty is not resolved even as the number of parameters is increased, suggesting that increasing model scale will not lead to robust search abilities.
notes: Fixed-depth decoder-only Transformers; no looped baseline. Supports hypothesis vs T0 but says nothing about T1.

claim: Search protocol detail: models trained on up to 883M examples with maximum input graph size of 41 vertices; naive vs star vs balanced training distributions compared.
quote: Accuracy of model with a maximum input graph size of 41 vertices trained on 883M examples from the naı̈ve distribution, vs star distribution, vs the balanced distribution with lookaheads L ≤ 20
notes: Pitfall: naive random-graph distributions let models shortcut; training distribution (lookahead balance) decides whether search is learned.

claim: Transformers learn an 'exponential path-merging' search: each layer extends per-vertex reachable sets, covering a number of vertices exponential in layer count.
quote: Each layer successively extends the sets of reachable vertices, thereby allowing the model to search over a number of vertices exponential in the number of layers.
notes: Attention already performs state-conditioned dynamic routing on graphs: the objection made concrete.

claim: Disentangled Transformer with L layers provably computes connectivity for graph diameter up to 3^L (powers of the adjacency matrix); beyond-capacity training graphs drive a node-degree heuristic.
unit: max diameter solvable by L layers
quote: an L-layer model can compute connectivity in graphs with diameters up to 3L , implementing an algorithm equivalent to computing powers of the adjacency matrix.
notes: Superscript lost in PDF text ('3L' = 3^L). Implies T1 needs ~log3(diameter) loops.

claim: Restricting training data to within-capacity graphs makes standard and Disentangled Transformers learn the exact connectivity algorithm; otherwise they learn a degree heuristic (shortcut).
quote: restricting training data to stay within a model’s capacity makes both standard and Disentangled Transformers learn the exact algorithm.
notes: Benchmark pitfall: reachability datasets admit degree-based shortcuts; train-diameter must be controlled per arm depth/iterations.

claim: Transformers learn connectivity on low-dimensional grid-like directed graphs but struggle on non-grid graphs with many disconnected components.
quote: if the graph is not a grid graph and contains many disconnected components, transformers struggle to learn the connectivity task, especially when the number of components is large.
notes: Under review per PDF header. Graph family is a confound for reachability benchmarks.

claim: Loukas 2019: many graph decision/optimisation problems are impossible for message-passing GNNs unless depth x width exceeds a polynomial of the graph size.
quote: several of these problems are deemed impossible unless the product of a GNNmp’s depth and width exceeds a polynomial of the graph size
notes: Depth (iterations T) and width trade off: fixed-width recurrent graph needs T growing polynomially in n for these tasks — compute grows even when parameters do not.

claim: Joshi 2025: Transformers are message-passing GNNs on fully connected token graphs, with attention giving relative importance of all tokens.
quote: We show how Transformers can be viewed as message passing GNNs operating on fully connected graphs of tokens, where the self-attention mechanism capture the relative importance of all tokens w.r.t. each-other
notes: The central objection, stated in the literature.

claim: Joshi 2025: Transformers run as dense matrix operations far more efficient on modern hardware than sparse message passing — 'GNNs currently winning the hardware lottery'.
quote: Transformers are implemented via dense matrix operations that are significantly more efficient on modern hardware than sparse message passing. This leads to the perspective that Transformers are GNNs currently winning the hardware lottery.
notes: Direct evidence relevant to V5 (wall-clock).

claim: Illusion of State: S4/Mamba-type SSMs, like Transformers, lie in TC0 and cannot solve permutation composition (S5 word problem) and related state tracking.
quote: the expressive power of S4, Mamba, and related SSMs is limited very similarly to transformers (within TC0 ), meaning these SSMs cannot solve simple state-tracking problems like permutation composition
notes: Under standard complexity conjecture (TC0 != NC1). Fixed-depth/log-precision assumption; looped models with depth growing with length escape this.

claim: Transformers Learn Shortcuts to Automata: an o(T)-layer Transformer can exactly simulate any finite-state automaton on length-T inputs; O(log T)-depth solutions always exist and O(1)-depth ones are common.
quote: We find that polynomial-sized O(log T )-depth solutions always exist; furthermore, O(1)-depth simulators are surprisingly common, and can be understood using tools from Krohn-Rhodes theory and circuit complexity.
notes: Recurrence over T steps is not needed for automata if log-depth parallel scan suffices.

claim: Shortcut solutions learned by Transformers on automata are brittle out of distribution.
quote: Empirically, we find that Transformers converge to shortcut solutions with standard training, across a wide variety of automata. We further investigate the brittleness of these solutions and propose potential mitigations.
notes: Pitfall: in-distribution success on state tracking may be a non-extrapolating shortcut; test longer lengths.

claim: Neural Networks and the Chomsky Hierarchy: 20,910 models on 15 tasks; train lengths 1-40, test 41-500; open-source generator.
quote: We define the maximum training sequence length as the training range N , with N = 40. Every mini-batch is generated by first sampling a length ` from the uniform distribution U(1, N )
notes: Generator: github.com/deepmind/neural_networks_chomsky_hierarchy. Test range U(N+1, M) with M = 500 stated in the same paragraph.

claim: Chomsky hierarchy result: RNNs and Transformers fail to generalise on non-regular tasks; LSTMs solve regular and counter tasks; only stack/tape-augmented nets generalise on context-free and context-sensitive tasks.
quote: RNNs and Transformers fail to generalize on non-regular tasks, LSTMs can solve regular and counter-language tasks, and only networks augmented with structured memory (such as a stack or memory tape) can successfully generalize
notes: Supports C9 (memory) necessity; recurrence alone (plain RNN) insufficient for non-regular tasks.

claim: Parallelism tradeoff: log-precision Transformers are in uniform TC0; if L != P they cannot accurately solve linear equalities or arbitrary CFG membership.
quote: if L 6= P (i.e., not all poly-time problems can be solved using logarithmic space), then transformers cannot even accurately solve linear equalities or check membership in an arbitrary context-free grammar
notes: '6=' is the PDF rendering of '≠'. Fixed-depth limit; recurrent depth escapes it.

claim: Linear RNNs (Mamba, RWKV, GLA, mLSTM, DeltaNet) and Transformers cannot solve even parity in one forward pass; allowing negative eigenvalues in state transitions fixes parity and extends state tracking.
quote: In one forward pass, current architectures are unable to solve even parity, the simplest state-tracking task, which non-linear RNNs can handle effectively.
notes: Recurrence alone is not enough: the update function's spectrum matters (relevant to U design).

claim: Permutation composition is a natural general state-tracking probe: automata simulation and boolean expression evaluation reduce to it.
quote: many other tasks (e.g., simulation of finite automata and evaluation of boolean expressions) can be reduced to permutation composition, making it a natural model for state tracking in general.
notes: Justifies S3/S5 word problem as the state-machine benchmark.

claim: Saunshi et al. 2025: a k-layer Transformer looped L times nearly matches a kL-layer non-looped model on addition, p-hop induction and math, and beats a k-layer model.
quote: a k-layer transformer looped L times nearly matches the performance of a kL-layer non-looped model, and is significantly better than a k-layer model.
notes: Iso-param (k-layer) and iso-FLOP (kL-layer) baselines both reported: the matching standard the program should copy. This is the T1 arm the candidate must beat.

claim: Looped LMs have worse perplexity and memorisation than iso-FLOP non-looped models but reasoning closer to iso-FLOP, despite L times fewer parameters.
quote: looped models have an inductive bias towards good reasoning despite having worse perplexity and memorization to an iso-flop non-looped model
notes: Direct evidence for separating computational capacity (recurrence helps) from knowledge storage (recurrence does not).

claim: Knowledge capacity scaling law: language models store at most about 2 bits of factual knowledge per parameter, even at int8.
quote: language models can and only can store 2 bits of knowledge per parameter, even when quantized to int8
notes: Storage bound depends on parameters, not iterations: recurrence cannot raise it. Measured on GPT-2/LLaMA/Mistral/MoE families, not looped models.

claim: Recurrent GNNs with finite-precision parameters, sum aggregation and ReLU can compute any graph algorithm respecting the Color-Refinement (1-WL) invariance.
quote: recurrent GNNs with finite-precision parameters, sum aggregation, and ReLU activation, can compute any graph algorithm that respects the natural message-passing invariance induced by the Color Refinement (or Weisfeiler-Leman) algorithm.
notes: Upper bound for C3/C4/C5 with fixed topology: recurrence reaches the 1-WL ceiling but not beyond; learned edges (C6) are a way to escape it.

claim: Recurrent-depth Transformers trained from scratch generalise systematically and extrapolate in hop depth (e.g. 5-hop train to 10-hop) by scaling inference-time recurrence, where vanilla Transformers struggle.
quote: For depth extrapolation, we show that generalization beyond training depth can be unlocked by scaling inference-time recurrence, with more iterations enabling deeper reasoning.
notes: Looped Transformer (T1) already extrapolates in depth — the bar the graph arm must clear.

claim: Mechanistic study of looped Transformers: both matched- and decoupled-recurrence variants become unreliable at greater depths; local errors persist and compound.
quote: both mechanisms become unreliable at greater depths: MR-Loop exhibits degradation of its readout state and progress cues, while DR-Loop exhibits declining reliability of state propagation. Limited self-correction allows local errors to persist and compound.
notes: Failure evidence for 'iterations replace depth' beyond training horizon in the T1 comparator; applies to any recurrent substrate.

claim: Discovering Neural Wirings: channels form connections independently of layers; the wiring is learned jointly with parameters during training (then fixed at inference).
quote: The wiring of our network is not fixed during training – as we learn the network parameters we also learn the structure itself.
notes: Topology learned ONCE (static after training), not per input or per iteration.

claim: DNW: learning MobileNetV1 connectivity raises ImageNet accuracy by 10% at about 41M FLOPs vs hand-engineered and random wirings.
quote: By learning the connectivity of MobileNetV1 [12] we boost the ImageNet accuracy by 10% at ∼ 41M FLOPs.
notes: FLOP-matched comparison (same ~41M FLOPs budget) against hand-designed MobileNetV1 at that budget.

claim: DNW 'dynamic neural graphs' let node states vary in time and contain cycles (expressing LSTMs); a 3-layer MLP equals a dynamic neural graph run for 3 time steps.
quote: Dynamic Neural Graph: A 3-layer perceptron (left) can be expressed by a dynamic neural graph with 3 time steps (right).
notes: Closest early formalisation of 'time replaces depth' on a learned-wiring graph (C1, C5).

claim: RigL trains sparse networks at fixed parameter count and fixed compute by periodically dropping low-magnitude and regrowing high-gradient connections.
quote: Our method updates the topology of the sparse network during training by using parameter magnitudes and infrequent gradient calculations.
notes: Topology learned during training, static at inference.

claim: RigL: ResNet-50 at 96.5% sparsity reaches 72.75% ImageNet top-1 with ERK sparsity distribution.
quote: For example ResNet-50 with 96.5% sparsity achieves a remarkable 72.75% Top-1 Accuracy
notes: Compared against dense ResNet-50 and pruning baselines; FLOP reduction is theoretical (unstructured sparsity), wall-clock not shown.

claim: SET evolves an initial Erdős-Rényi sparse topology between layers into a scale-free topology during training, reducing parameters quadratically without accuracy loss.
quote: an algorithm which evolves an initial sparse topology (Erdős-Rényi random graph) of two consecutive layers of neurons into a scale-free topology, during learning. Our method replaces artificial neural networks fully-connected layers with sparse ones before training, reducing quadratically the number of parameters
notes: Static after training.

claim: Weight Agnostic NNs: architecture search where all connections share a single random weight; topologies alone solve RL tasks and reach above-chance MNIST.
quote: To evaluate these networks, we populate the connections with a single shared weight parameter sampled from a uniform random distribution, and measure the expected performance.
notes: Topology carries computation with ~1 parameter: an extreme 'topology is computation' datapoint, but weak tasks.

claim: Randomly wired networks from classical random-graph generators reach competitive ImageNet accuracy.
quote: several variants of these random generators yield network instances that have competitive accuracy on the ImageNet benchmark.
notes: Adversarial: if random wiring is competitive, learned wiring's marginal value is small; G2 vs G1 (V2) must control for random sparse graphs.

claim: Recurrent Independent Mechanisms: groups of recurrent cells with nearly independent dynamics, communicating sparingly via attention and competing so only the most relevant are updated each step.
quote: multiple groups of recurrent cells operate with nearly independent transition dynamics, communicate only sparingly through the bottleneck of attention, and compete with each other so they are updated only at time steps where they are most relevant.
notes: Per-step, state-conditioned top-k activation (C6/C8) over modules; communication graph is attention (dense among active).

claim: RIMs: only top-k_A of k_T modules are activated per step by input attention; non-activated RIMs keep their state unchanged.
quote: individual activated RIMs follow their own default transition dynamics while non-activated RIMs remain unchanged. In the fourth stage, the RIMs sparsely communicate information between themselves, also using key-value attention.
notes: Persistent node state (C1) with sparse updates.

claim: RIMs copying task: trained on length 50, tested on 200; RIMs reach 0.00 test cross-entropy vs LSTM 3.56 and Transformers 0.54.
notes: Quote is PDF reading-order of the table. Parameter counts of baselines not matched in table.

claim: RIMs sequential-MNIST resolution transfer: trained 14x14, RIMs (kA=4) reach 38.1% at 24x24 vs LSTM 21.9% (hsize 600).
notes: Training resolution stated in the paper's Sec. 4 text (14x14). hsize matched at 600 (approximate param matching).

claim: Neural Production Systems: rule templates bound to entity slots; rules are scored for match and the best-fitting rules update entity properties; motivated by GNNs not predisposing sparse interactions.
quote: Rules are scored on their match to entities, and the best fitting rules are applied to update entity properties.
notes: Per-step state-conditioned sparse selection of (rule, entity) pairs: C6/C8 prior art.

claim: NPS authors: GNNs do not predispose interactions to be sparse nor factorise interaction knowledge entity-conditionally.
quote: First, GNNs do not predispose interactions to be sparse, as relationships among independent entities are likely to be. Second, GNNs do not factorize knowledge about interactions in an entity-conditional manner.

claim: Shared Global Workspace: specialist modules communicate through a bandwidth-limited shared workspace, competing for write access, replacing pairwise interactions.
quote: The proposed method includes a shared workspace through which communication among different specialist modules takes place but due to limits on the communication bandwidth, specialist modules must compete for access.
notes: Hub-node (star/hyperedge-like) communication: an alternative to sparse pairwise edges, relevant to C7.

claim: Shared workspace authors: capacity limits encourage specialisation and compositionality and help synchronise specialists.
quote: We show that capacity limitations have a rational basis in that (1) they encourage specialization and compositionality and (2) they facilitate the synchronization of otherwise independent specialists.

claim: HyperNetworks: a small network generates the weights of a larger one; viewed as relaxed weight-sharing across layers; fewer learnable parameters on convnets.
quote: hypernetworks can be viewed as relaxed form of weight-sharing across layers. Our main result is that hypernetworks can generate non-shared weights for LSTM
notes: Middle ground between full sharing (C3/C4) and per-step weights.

claim: Graph HyperNetworks generate weights for a given architecture by running a GNN over the architecture's computation graph, amortising NAS.
quote: we propose the Graph HyperNetwork (GHN) to amortize the search cost: given an architecture, it directly generates the weights by running inference on a graph neural network.
notes: Topology as input to weight generation; topology fixed per evaluated network.

claim: Top-KAST keeps training fully parameter-sparse: never a dense forward pass nor a dense gradient.
quote: Our technique is scalable because it never requires doing a forward pass with dense parameters, nor calculating a dense gradient.
notes: Top-k over weight magnitudes (static per step), not over node states.

claim: Cannistraci-Hebb training (2025): gradient-free topology-driven link regrowth in dynamic sparse training; with 5% of connections it outperforms fully connected networks on two Transformer machine-translation tasks.
quote: Using 5% of the connections, CHTss outperforms fully connected networks in two Transformer-based machine translation tasks.
notes: Param-matched? No: sparse model has fewer active params than the dense baseline. Topology static at inference.

claim: CHT authors state prior CHT time complexity is O(N·d^3) and introduce a matrix-multiplication GPU-friendly approximation of the link predictor.
quote: CHT suffers two main drawbacks: (i) its time complexity is O(N · d3 )- N node network size, d node degree
notes: Topology-learning cost itself can dominate on GPU.

claim: Resonant Sparse Geometry Networks (2026): nodes embedded in learned hyperbolic space with input-dependent sparse connectivity, O(n·k) cost; claims 96.5% on long-range dependency tasks with ~15x fewer parameters than Transformers.
quote: RSGN achieves 96.5% accuracy on long-range dependency tasks while using approximately 15× fewer parameters than standard Transformers.
notes: Single-author preprint, synthetic tasks, baseline not param-matched; parameter-efficiency claim unverified.

claim: RSGN on 20-class hierarchical classification: 23.8% with 41,672 params vs Transformer 30.1% with 403,348 params, i.e. lower accuracy than the Transformer.
quote: RSGN achieves 23.8% accuracy (compared to 5% random baseline) with only 41,672 parameters, nearly 10× fewer than Transformer baselines requiring 403,348 parameters to achieve 30.1% accuracy.
notes: Unmatched (10x params difference); the brain-like sparse graph loses on accuracy. Counter-evidence to the 2026 'brain-like substrate' claims.

claim: The Hardware Lottery: ideas win because they suit available hardware/software, not because they are superior; GPUs/TPUs are optimised for dense matrix multiplies.
quote: This essay introduces the term hardware lottery to describe when a research idea wins because it is suited to the available software and hardware and not because the idea is superior to alternative research directions.
notes: Frames V5: sparse dynamic graphs may lose on wall-clock even if they win on FLOPs.

claim: Slot Attention: exchangeable slots bind to input objects via competition over multiple rounds of iterative attention (persistent slot states, shared update).
quote: These slots are exchangeable and can bind to any object in the input by specializing through a competitive procedure over multiple rounds of attention.
notes: Iterative shared-weight node updates with competitive (softmax-over-slots) routing.

claim: Continuous Thought Machine (2025): neuron-level temporal processing with per-neuron weights over activation histories, and neural synchronisation as the latent representation.
quote: The CTM has two innovations: (1) neuron-level temporal processing, where each neuron uses unique weight parameters to process incoming histories; and (2) neural synchronization as a latent representation.
notes: Per-neuron (not shared) weights: violates C3/C4 sharing. R3 covers in depth.

claim: CTM solves 39x39 mazes trained up to 100 steps and generalises to 99x99 by sequential re-application.
quote: Solving 100 steps down 39 × 39 mazes. (a, b) Observing using attention (no positional encoding, weights overlaid), imagining a route (arrows) from red to green pixels, (b) attending beyond 100 steps, and (c) generalizing to 99 × 99 via sequential re-application
notes: Re-application = running the model repeatedly on crops; not a single-pass extrapolation. No matched baseline in caption.

claim: Sparse Growing Transformer (2026): training-time sparse depth allocation that progressively extends recurrence (attention looping) to informative heads.
quote: SGT is a trainingtime sparse depth allocation framework that progressively extends recurrence from deeper to shallower layers via targeted attention looping on informative heads.
notes: Learned sparse recurrence inside a Transformer: a looped-Transformer variant that already allocates iterations sparsely.

claim: Zoology: 82% of the perplexity gap between attention and gated-convolution LMs is explained by associative recall; a 70M attention model beats a 1.4B gated-convolution model on AR.
unit: % of perplexity gap explained by AR
quote: In fine-grained analysis, we find 82% of the gap is explained by each model’s ability to recall information that is previously mentioned in-context
notes: Unmatched (70M vs 1.4B) by design: shows recall is architecture-, not parameter-, limited.

claim: MQAR (multi-query associative recall) defined to reflect language: multiple recalls in one forward pass, varying positions, vocabulary larger than model dimension.
quote: We thus propose the study of multi-query AR (Mqar). Compared to the prior AR formulations, Mqar better captures the persisting quality gaps on synthetic and real world data
notes: Generator in HazyResearch/zoology repo (license checked separately).

claim: MQAR theory: gated-convolution (BaseConv) model dimension must grow with sequence length to solve MQAR, while attention solves it with dimension independent of length.
quote: the model dimension for BaseConv (and thus the aforementioned architectures) to solve Mqar grows with the input sequence length (Theorem 4.4) while attention can solve Mqar with model dimension independent of sequence length
notes: Attention is a strong associative-recall baseline; a sparse top-k graph must match it on MQAR.

claim: Recurrent Relational Network on Sudoku: 81 cell-nodes, edges within row/column/box (fixed graph), shared message function, trained for 32 steps; 216,000 puzzles with 17-34 givens.
quote: We run the network for 32 steps and at every step the output function r maps each node hidden state to nine output logits corresponding to the nine possible digits.
notes: Closest prior art for C1/C3/C4/C5/C10 (readout at every node, every step) on a fixed constraint graph.

claim: RRN trained for 32 steps improves when run for 64 steps at test: accuracy on hardest (17-given) Sudokus rises to 96.6%.
quote: The model was trained for 32 steps, but seeing that the accuracy increased with more steps, we ran the model for 64 steps during testing. At 64 steps the accuracy for the 17 givens puzzles increases to 96.6%.
notes: Direct evidence for V4 (more iterations beyond T_train help, 2x). Baselines are other Sudoku solvers, not a Transformer; unmatched.

claim: SATNet: differentiable MAXSAT layer learns 9x9 Sudoku solely from examples and a visual Sudoku variant.
quote: we show that we can learn the parity function using single-bit supervision (a traditionally hard task for deep networks) and learn how to play 9 × 9 Sudoku solely from examples.
notes: A follow-up critique (symbol grounding / label leakage in visual Sudoku) is listed under unconfirmed leads.

claim: ARC: benchmark built on explicit human-like priors measuring skill-acquisition efficiency; argues unlimited priors or data let systems 'buy' skill.
quote: unlimited priors or unlimited training data allow experimenters to “buy” arbitrary levels of skills for a system, in a way that masks the system’s own generalization power.
notes: Methodological argument for matching training data and priors across arms.

claim: ARC-AGI-1: 400 public training and 400 public evaluation tasks; 100-task private and 100-task semi-private evaluation sets; repeated leaderboard submission risks overfitting to the 100 hidden tasks.
quote: The original public dataset contained 400 training tasks and 400 evaluation tasks. A Private Evaluation set of 100 tasks was reserved for competition leaderboards
notes: Pitfall named in the same paper: leaderboard feedback loop tunes to idiosyncrasies of hidden tasks.

claim: SCAN length split: train on commands with action sequences up to 22 actions (16,990 commands), test on longer; best seq2seq (attention GRU) only 20.8% on average.
quote: This test turns out to be very challenging for all models. The best result (20.8% on average, again over 5 runs) is achieved by a GRU with attention, one 50-dimensional hidden layer, and dropout 0.5.
notes: 2017 RNN baselines only; no Transformer/looped in this paper.

claim: COGS: Transformers and LSTMs reach 96-99% in-distribution but only 16-35% on the compositional generalisation set, with ±6-8% seed sensitivity.
quote: in-distribution accuracy on the COGS test set was near-perfect (96– 99%), but generalization accuracy was substantially lower (16–35%) and showed high sensitivity to random seed (±6–8%).
notes: Seed variance ±6-8% means >=3 seeds is a minimum; prereg's 3 seeds may be underpowered on COGS-type tasks.

claim: CLUTRR: a GNN (GAT) on symbolic kinship graphs generalises to held-out rule combinations and is more robust than BERT/MAC on text.
quote: a graph neural network model that works directly with symbolic inputs—with the graph-based model exhibiting both stronger generalization and greater robustness.
notes: Unfair input: GNN gets the symbolic graph, text models get stories — input modality, not architecture, may explain the gap.

claim: Paradox of learning to reason: BERT reaches near-perfect in-distribution accuracy on SimpleLogic but fails on other distributions over the same problem space by learning statistical features.
quote: BERT attains near-perfect accuracy on in-distribution test examples while failing to generalize to other data distributions over the exact same problem space.
notes: Benchmark pitfall: generator sampling choices create shortcut features; test with multiple generators.

claim: Easy-to-hard datasets: Prefix Sums, Mazes, and Chess Puzzles packaged as a pip-installable Python package for training easy / testing hard.
quote: We present three datasets: Prefix Sums, Mazes, and Chess Puzzles. We also provide an easy to install Python package and accompanying documentation
notes: Package easy-to-hard-data; repo/license checked in CODE rows.

claim: maze-dataset library: configurable maze generation algorithms, parameters and filters; rasterised and text outputs for CNNs and autoregressive Transformers.
quote: it supports multiple output formats, including rasterized and text-based, catering to convolutional neural networks and autoregressive transformer models.
notes: Supports percolation (cycles) and deadend-start shifts used by 2410.03020.

claim: Searchformer: encoder-decoder Transformer trained on A* search traces optimally solves unseen Sokoban puzzles 93.7% of the time with up to 26.8% fewer search steps than A*.
quote: a Transformer model that optimally solves previously unseen Sokoban puzzles 93.7% of the time, while using up to 26.8% fewer search steps than the A∗ implementation that was used for training initially.
notes: Relies on long search-trace token sequences (inference compute not matched to non-trace baselines).

claim: TRM: Sudoku-Extreme has only 1K training samples and 423K test samples (9x9); Maze-Hard is 30x30 with shortest path length above 110, 1000 train and 1000 test mazes.
quote: Sudoku-Extreme consists of extremely difficult Sudoku puzzles (Dillion, 2025; Palm et al., 2018; Park, 2018) (9x9 grid), for which only 1K training samples are used to test small-sample learning. Testing is done on 423K samples.
notes: Fixed-size tasks: no size extrapolation axis, so they cannot measure n* (prereg primary metric).

claim: TRM (7M params) reaches 74.7% Sudoku-Extreme and 85.3% Maze-Hard vs HRM (27M) 55.0% and 74.5%; LLMs with CoT (DeepSeek R1, Claude 3.7, o3-mini-high) score 0.0 on both.
quote: TRM-Att (Ours) 7M 74.7 85.3
notes: Param-unmatched (7M vs 27M vs 671B); TRM-MLP gets 87.4 on Sudoku but 0.0 on Maze (Table 4) - architecture choice is task-specific.

claim: TRM-MLP (no self-attention) solves 87.4% of Sudoku-Extreme but 0.0% of Maze-Hard.
quote: TRM-MLP (Ours) 5M/19M 1 87.4 0.0
notes: PDF text renders footnote marker '1'; row reads 87.4 Sudoku, 0.0 Maze. Evidence that the communication pattern (attention vs fixed MLP mixing) is task-dependent.

claim: TRM reports ARC-AGI-1 44.6% and ARC-AGI-2 7.8% with 7M parameters vs HRM 40.3% and 5.0% at 27M.
quote: TRM with self-attention obtains 85.3% accuracy on Maze-Hard, 44.6% accuracy on ARC-AGI-1, and 7.8% accuracy on ARC-AGI-2 with 7M parameters.
notes: Unmatched params; ARC numbers use test-time augmentation/voting per HRM protocol.

claim: TRM author notes HRM's fixed-point (implicit-gradient) justification is unsupported: no guarantee a fixed point is reached.
quote: There are concerns about applying this theorem to HRM. Most importantly, there is no guarantee that a fixed-point is reached.
notes: Convergence claims need measurement (state-norm / residual), relevant to C11 and V4.

claim: Efficiency Misnomer: parameter count alone is misleading; a model with few trainable parameters can be slow when parameters are shared across many computational steps.
quote: a model can have very few trainable parameters and still be very slow, for instance when the parameters are shared among many computational steps (Lan et al., 2019; Dehghani et al., 2018).
notes: Direct criticism of param-only matching for weight-shared/recurrent models; supports prereg's report-all-costs rule.

claim: Efficiency Misnomer Figure 1: ranking of Transformer, Universal Transformer and Switch Transformer reverses depending on whether parameters, FLOPs or throughput is the cost axis.
quote: Comparison of standard Transformers, Universal Transformers and Switch Transformers in terms of three common cost metrics: number of parameters, FLOPs, and throughput. Relative ranking between models is reversed between the two cost indicators.
notes: Measured on 64 TPU-v3 with Mesh TensorFlow.

claim: Efficiency Misnomer: parameter-shared models save inference memory, but training activation memory for the backward pass is as large as for an unshared model of equal depth.
quote: during training, the size of activation that need to be kept for the backward pass is just as large as for a similar model with no parameter sharing.
notes: BPTT through T iterations costs O(T) activation memory regardless of sharing: report peak memory.

claim: MoEUT: layer-shared Universal Transformers drastically cut parameters vs an unshared model of equal dimension; scaling width to compensate makes compute prohibitive.
quote: layer-sharing comes with a practical limitation of parameter-compute ratio: it drastically reduces the parameter count compared to the non-shared model with the same dimensionality.
notes: The parameter-compute ratio problem applies to any weight-shared graph substrate (shared M/U).

claim: MoEUT matching practice: parameter-matched to dense baselines (same d_model and n_layers) and compares on both parameter and training-MAC axes; MoEUT slightly beats parameter-matched dense models on C4.
quote: MoEUT slightly outperforms parameter-matched models with no layer sharing. The gap grows with scale. (b) Given equal amounts of compute, MoEUT outperforms other models by a large margin.
notes: Template for dual (param + MAC) matched reporting.

claim: MoEUT trains 1.5-2x slower than a standard Transformer with FlashAttention because its Triton MoE kernel is suboptimal.
quote: Compared to the standard Transformer with FlashAttention [56], our MoEUT model trains 1.5–2x slower.
notes: Sparse/conditional compute pays a wall-clock tax on GPUs even when MAC-matched: V5 evidence.

claim: Looped Transformers for length generalisation (ICLR 2025): Parity trained on lengths [1,20] generalises to more than 40 digits near perfectly with adaptive loop count; NTP baselines fail at max training length +10 on addition and copy.
quote: for Parity, it can generalize to more than 40 digits near perfectly when trained with up to 20 digits.
notes: Requires ground-truth step count T(n) in training data (step-dependent supervision). Baselines NTP, NTP-Pause, NTP-Loop: not FLOP-matched.

claim: Equilibrium Reasoners (2026): iterative latent models trained with max 16 iterations scale test-time compute by more iterations and by aggregating stochastic trajectories; gains are tied to convergence to attractors.
quote: More Iterations Training Max Iters = 16 We formalize this process by introducing Equilibrium Reasoners (EqR).
notes: Figure text fragment; supports C11 (convergence signal) as a test-time compute controller. Code github.com/locuslab/EqR.

claim: ARC Prize analysis of HRM: a regular Transformer with the same ~27M parameters and the same pipeline comes within ~5pp of HRM without hyperparameter tuning.
locator: Section on Finding 1 (HRM vs Transformer, Figure 3)
quote: a regular transformer comes within ~5pp of the HRM model without any hyperparameter optimization.
notes: Param-matched (~27M both, stated on page). Strong evidence that the brain-inspired structure adds little over a weight-matched Transformer in the same recurrent pipeline.

claim: ARC Prize HRM analysis: the outer refinement loop drives performance: going from no refinement (1 loop) to 1 refinement adds +13pp; 1 to 8 loops doubles public-eval performance.
unit: pp gain from first refinement loop
quote: from no refinement (1 loop) to just 1 refinement, performance jumps by +13pp. From 1 to 8 refinement loops, the Public Evaluation set performance doubles.
notes: Iteration (time) is what helps — consistent with 'recurrence, not graph/hierarchy'.

claim: ARC Prize HRM analysis: training with more refinement steps improves single-loop inference by >15pp; extra refinement loops at inference matter less.
quote: Training with more refinement improves the performance of predictions with a single refinement loop by >15pp, even though one loop means a single forward pass without any refinement.
notes: Adversarial for V4: benefit of recurrence is largely a training-time effect (deep supervision), not test-time extra iterations.

claim: ARC Prize: HRM is purely transductive (puzzle-id conditioned, inference data part of training set); most performance comes from memorising solutions to evaluation tasks.
quote: Cross-task transfer learning has limited benefits; most of the performance comes from memorizing solutions to the specific tasks used at evaluation time.
notes: Benchmark pitfall for ARC-style evals: transductive puzzle-id training leaks test tasks into training.

claim: ARC Prize verified HRM semi-private scores: ARC-AGI-1 32%, ARC-AGI-2 2%.
quote: HRM shows impressive performance for its size on the ARC-AGI Semi-Private sets: ARC-AGI-1: 32%
notes: Lower than HRM's self-reported public numbers; held-out evaluation matters.

claim: TRM on ARC-AGI-1 (2025 note): 1000-sample augmentation voting adds 10.75pp Pass@1; replacing the puzzle ID with a blank or random token gives zero accuracy.
quote: the 1000-sample voting pipeline improves Pass@1 by 10.75 percentage points over single-pass canonical inference. Second, a puzzle-identity ablation reveals strict dependence on task identifiers
notes: Independent re-analysis of the released TRM checkpoint. Pitfall: identity conditioning + test-time augmentation inflate ARC numbers.

claim: Same TRM note: most of final accuracy is achieved at the first recursion step.
quote: Third, a recursion trajectory analysis shows that most of the final accuracy is achieved at the first recursion step
notes: Adversarial: recursion depth contributes little at inference on ARC-AGI-1.

claim: SATNet failure: without intermediate labels mapping digit images to symbols, SATNet gets 0% test accuracy on visual Sudoku (symbol grounding failure; original result relied on label leakage).
unit: % test accuracy, visual Sudoku without intermediate labels
quote: in the absence of intermediate labels that identify individual Sudoku digit images with their logical representations, SATNet completely fails at visual Sudoku (0% test accuracy).
notes: Failed-replication/pitfall row. NeurIPS 2020 per the proceedings review page found in search; arXiv posted 2023.

claim: Looped Transformer with extra graph-attention heads provably simulates Dijkstra, BFS, DFS and Kosaraju SCC with parameter count independent of graph size, limited by finite precision.
quote: The number of parameters in the networks does not increase with the input graph size, which implies that the networks can simulate the above algorithms for any graph. Despite this property, we show a limit to simulation in our solution due to finite precision.
notes: A looped Transformer (T1 + graph attention) already has constant-parameter algorithmic capacity on graphs: the candidate's capacity-per-parameter advantage over T1 is not guaranteed by expressivity.

claim: Construction detail: a 17-layer, 3-head, O(1)-width looped Transformer simulates Dijkstra up to O(1/δ) nodes (precision-limited).
quote: with 17 layers, 3 attention heads, and layer width O(1) that simulates Dijkstra’s shortest path algorithm for weighted graphs with rational edge-weights
notes: Graph size bounded by precision δ, not by parameters.

claim: Relational Transformer (attention updating edge vectors) averages 66.60% OOD on CLRS-30 classes vs tuned MPNN 49.23% and PGN-c 52.83%.
notes: Columns Deep Sets, GAT-v1, GAT-v2, MPNN, PGN-u, PGN-m, PGN-c, RT. All tuned; parameter counts not matched (RT adds edge-update params).

claim: On 8 core CLRS algorithms a standard Transformer (re-tuned) averages 42.34% OOD vs 81.30% for the Relational Transformer that adds edge vectors.
unit: % OOD average, standard Transformer (8 core algorithms)
notes: Ablation within same codebase, hyperparameters re-tuned; parameter count not reported as matched. Shows plain dense attention without edge state is weak on CLRS OOD.

claim: RT authors: published CLRS-30 MPNN score drops from 96.63% validation (16 nodes) to 51.02% test (64 nodes).
quote: MPNN’s average evaluation score drops from 96.63% on the validation set to 51.02% on the test set.
notes: Size-generalisation gap quantified.

claim: Mechanistic study of HRM (2026): ablating the high-level state zH at all steps reduces Sudoku cell accuracy by 19.3%; prior work called HRM a 'structured guesser' with fixed-point violations.
quote: We find that ablating zH at all steps reduces cell accuracy significantly (-19.3%), with per-step effect increasing
notes: Relevant to C11: fixed points are not reliably reached in HRM-style recurrent reasoners.

claim: Iteration budget asymmetry on reachability: message passing along task edges needs T >= diameter steps, while an L-layer (or L-loop) attention model covers diameter 3^L; for a 64-node path graph that is 63 message-passing steps vs 4 attention layers/loops.
unit: steps (MP on task graph) vs layers (attention), path graph n=64
locator: Abstract (3^L capacity) applied to a path graph
quote: an L-layer model can compute connectivity in graphs with diameters up to 3L , implementing an algorithm equivalent to computing powers of the adjacency matrix.
notes: T_MP = diam = n-1 = 63; L_attn = ceil(log3(63)) = 4 (3^4=81>=63). Implication for prereg: matching 'iterations' across G1-G3 and T1 is not compute-neutral on reachability; a graph arm without learned long-range edges (C6) needs ~16x more iterations here.

claim: Size-ladder implication: with n_train=16, CLRS-30's single test size (64) reaches only the prereg's minimum 4x ratio, while SALSA-CLRS offers rungs 80/160/800/1600 (5x-100x).
quote: SALSA-CLRS enables the evaluation of scalable architectures on graphs up to 100 times the size of the training graphs.
notes: Ratios = {80,160,800,1600}/16 = {5,10,50,100}; CLRS-30: 64/16 = 4. Recommend SALSA-style ladder for reachability/shortest path.

claim: Recurrent GNNs with random node initialisation can emulate any polynomial-time graph algorithm on connected graphs in polynomial time; non-recurrent GNNs need a different network per graph size.
quote: In particular, any polynomial-time graph algorithm can be emulated on connected graphs in polynomial time by a recurrent GNN with random initialization.
notes: Expressivity support for 'time replaces depth' on a fixed graph substrate (C5); says nothing about learnability or sample efficiency.

claim: Looped Transformers can simulate hypergraph algorithms: a degradation mechanism reduces hypergraphs to graphs (e.g. Dijkstra) and a hyperedge-aware encoding simulates hypergraph-specific algorithms (Helly's algorithm), with theoretical guarantees.
quote: we propose a novel degradation mechanism for reducing hypergraphs to graph representations, enabling the simulation of graph-based algorithms, such as Dijkstra’s shortest path. Furthermore, we introduce a hyperedge-aware encoding scheme to simulate hypergraph-specific algorithms
notes: Hyperedges (C7) are already reachable by a looped Transformer at constant parameters; construction-level, no learned-from-data results.

claim: HyperGNN theory: enumerative training on examples up to a fixed graph size can ensure the trained network generalises to all larger graphs (fixed-precision setting).
quote: applying enumerative training with examples up to some fixed graph size can ensure that the trained neural network will generalize to all graphs larger than those appearing in the training set.
notes: Extended abstract. Size-generalisation guarantee for hypergraph (neural logic machine) models.

claim: Ouro looped LMs (LoopLM): controlled physics-of-LMs experiments find recurrence does not increase raw knowledge storage (about 2 bits per parameter for looped and non-looped) but improves knowledge manipulation (fact composition, multi-hop).
quote: we find recurrence does not increase raw knowledge storage (approximately 2 bits per parameter for looped and non-looped models) but dramatically enhances knowledge manipulation capabilities
notes: Param-matched comparison by design (bits/param). Directly confirms the prereg split: recurrence adds computation, not storage. Any graph substrate with shared M/U inherits the same storage ceiling.

claim: Iso-depth scaling law for looped LMs: looping a block r times is worth about r^0.46 unique blocks in validation loss (phi = 1 would be full equivalence, phi = 0 no capacity gain)
quote: we fit a joint scaling law L = E + A (Nonce + rφ Nrec )−α + B D−β and measure a recurrence-equivalence exponent φ = 0.46.
notes: Language-modelling validation loss, r in {1,2,4,8}, ~50x compute sweep.
